newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-BOSMAN RULING THREATENS FUTURE OF GERMAN GAME.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-BOSMAN RULING THREATENS FUTURE OF GERMAN GAME.

text.p: Germany is confident of getting European backing to host the World Cup in 2006. But the biggest problem for the European champions in the next decade will be finding enough talented young players to put up a decent show.

National team coach Berti Vogts, who led the country to last year's European championship triumph in England, believes the increasing number of foreign players in the Bundesliga after the controversial Bosman ruling is stifling talent.

"The consequences of this ruling have been worse than my worst fears," Vogts said. "They have gone right to the core of German football. The professional clubs have got to change their direction. Otherwise there is no future for our talented youngsters."

On the surface German football looks in good shape. This week Borussia Dortmund and Schalke will represent the country in the European Cup and UEFA Cup semifinals respectively. The national team still look a good bet for next year's World Cup.
But the future looks far from rosy after 1998 when key players such as national team captain and striker Juergen Klinsmann and defender Juergen Kohler are due to retire from the international game.
Vogts says today's teenagers, who should become the stars of the new millennium, are not getting a chance to break through in the Bundesliga.
The country's under-21 squad should be full of the players who will become household names in 2006. But the squad's coach Hannes Loehr recently produced some startling statistics.
"The present 26 players in the under-21 squad have been on the field for on average of 71 seconds per game in the German first and second divisions this season," Loehr said.

"The shocking fact is that most of them are lucky if they get on the bench...The under-21 situation is dramatic. The boom in foreign players, the most serious consequence of the Bosman ruling, means even our best young professionals are hardly getting a game in the Bundesliga."
On average foreign players made up more than a third of Bundesliga line-ups during the first half of the season, according to German soccer federation (DFB) statistics.

At times championship challengers VfB Stuttgart put more foreigners on the field than Germans. Borussia Moenchengladbach, Cologne, Bayer Leverkusen and Hamburg have fielded some of the highest percentages of foreign players.

"The share of under-21 players getting a game in the first division is, on average, 2.6 per cent, compared to 34.6 per cent for foreign players," Loehr said. "In the second division the relationship is 5.02 to 27.6 percent."

The Germans are expecting European ruling body UEFA to back their bid for the 2006 tournament, rather then England's, when they meet in Switzerland on April 17. World governing body FIFA makes the final decision but UEFA support is crucial.
Getting Bundesliga teams to play German youngsters rather than foreign imports is going to need a great deal more persuasion, however.
"I believe in top-class foreigners but it would be better to give our talent a chance rather than play average foreigners," Vogts said.
Vogts, a key member of the team which won the World Cup the last time it was held on German soil in 1974, does not have very long to solve the problem.

Most of the players who won Euro 96 will be on the wrong side of 30 by next year's World Cup finals in France. In some positions there are no youngsters making a serious challenge to replace the veterans.
